The remaining issue is cache: B is 2MB and doesn't fit L2, so I'm thinking about blocking over j and also over k while keeping k strictly ascending within each block, so the accumulation order for C[i][j] stays the same as the naive triple loop.\n\nWriting tiled matmul kernel...\n\nI'm thinking about block size tradeoffs for row-block parallelism: with N=512 and BI=64 I'd only get 8 chunks, which could leave threads idle if there are more than 8; I'm weighing BI=16 or BI=32 to get better load balance while keeping the A-row working set small enough for cache.\n\nI'm also checking that the accumulation order inside the blocked loops still matches the original sequential summation over k, since FMA contraction with -march=native should behave the same way in both versions and preserve numerical equivalence.\n\nFor pointer writes, I'll use __restrict to help the compiler vectorize cleanly. The initialization loop can be parallelized with OpenMP since getPseudoRndValue is a pure function, while validation stays serial since it's only computing 25 cheap dot products—no need for reduction there. cat > $T/cmp.cpp <<'EOF'\n#include <vector>\n#include <cstdio>\n#include <cstring>\n#include <cstddef>\n#include <algorithm>\n#include <cmath>\nconstexpr double getPseudoRndValue(const size_t N, const size_t i, const size_t j) noexcept {\n    return (((i + 1) * (i + j + 1) * 1299709) % (N * N)) / static_cast<double>(N * N);\n}\nvoid initMatrix(std::vector<double>& mat, const size_t N) {\n    for (size_t i = 0; i < N; ++i) for (size_t j = 0; j < N; ++j) mat[i * N + j] = getPseudoRndValue(N, i, j);\n}\nvoid ref(const std::vector<double>& A, const std::vector<double>& B, std::vector<double>& C, const size_t N) {\n    for (size_t i = 0; i < N; ++i) for (size_t j = 0; j < N; ++j) { double sum = 0.0;\n        for (size_t k = 0; k < N; ++k) sum += A[i * N + k] * B[k * N + j];\n        C[i * N + j] = sum; }\n}\nvoid tiled(const std::vector<double>& A, const std::vector<double>& B, std::vector<double>& C, const size_t N) {\n    constexpr size_t BI = 16, BJ = 256, BK = 128;\n    const double* __restrict a = A.data(); const double* __restrict b = B.data(); double* __restrict c = C.data();\n    for (size_t i0 = 0; i0 < N; i0 += BI) { size_t i1 = std::min(i0 + BI, N);\n        for (size_t i = i0; i < i1; ++i) std::fill(c + i * N, c + i * N + N, 0.0);\n        for (size_t j0 = 0; j0 < N; j0 += BJ) { size_t j1 = std::min(j0 + BJ, N);\n            for (size_t k0 = 0; k0 < N; k0 += BK) { size_t k1 = std::min(k0 + BK, N);\n                for (size_t i = i0; i < i1; ++i) { double* __restrict crow = c + i * N;\n                    for (size_t k = k0;   // rows of C per task\n    constexpr size_t BJ = 256;  // columns of C per tile\n    constexpr size_t BK = 128;  // inner-dimension tile\n\n    const double* __restrict a = A.data();\n    const double* __restrict b = B.data();\n    double* __restrict c = C.data();\n\n    const size_t numRowBlocks = (N + BI - 1) / BI;\n\n    #pragma omp parallel for schedule(static)\n    for (size_t rb = 0; rb < numRowBlocks; ++rb) {\n        const size_t i0 = rb * BI;\n        const size_t i1 = std::min(i0 + BI, N);\n\n        for (size_t i = i0; i < i1; ++i) {\n            std::fill(c + i * N, c + i * N + N, 0.0);\n        }\n\n        for (size_t j0 = 0; r < MR; ++r) {\n        for (size_t q = 0; q < NR; ++q) {\n            acc[r][q] = c[r * N + q];\n        }\n    }\n    for (size_t k = k0; k < k1; ++k) {\n        const double* __restrict brow = b + k * N;\n        for (size_t r = 0; r < MR; ++r) {\n            const double ar = a[r * N + k];\n            for (size_t q = 0; q < NR; ++q) {\n                acc[r][q] += ar * brow[q];\n            }\n        }\n    }\n    for (size_t r = 0; The likely culprit is the B column access pattern, where the stride per k-step spans a large memory footprint that's hurting cache behavior.\n\nThat stride is a power-of-two value, which is a classic recipe for cache set conflicts — every k touches a different set and causes aliasing. The fix is to pack B into a contiguous panel layout before the micro-kernel runs, so reads are sequential instead of strided. I'm planning a global packing pass that reshapes B into fixed-width column panels (padded to a multiple of NR), done once up front as a cheap O(N²) copy, so the micro-kernel can then stream through Bp contiguously with a tiny stride.\n\nI'll only pack and run the microkernel on full panels, handling leftover columns at the edge with a separate update path against the original B, since padding and packing those is wasted effort. The panel layout keeps k-contiguous blocks small and cache-friendly, and I can parallelize the packing step itself with a parallel loop over panels, accepting the modest extra memory for the temporary buffer since it's negligible next to the O(N³) work.\n\n","time":{"start":1793101781021,"end":1793101788571},"metadata":{"anthropic":{"signature":""}}}}

{"type":"reasoning","timestamp":1793101928071,"sessionID":"ses_e82d0d703ffeCXd4cjTWZV8YjR","part":{"id":"prt_17d33fdb4001hGZIbyMQjXMO2j","messageID":"msg_17d33f9300017aMbIjniODm4ev","sessionID":"ses_e82d0d703ffeCXd4cjTWZV8YjR","type":"reasoning","text":"Single-threaded, the new version beats the simple one, but oddly the simple kernel pulls ahead with multiple threads. I suspect this comes down to task granularity versus thread count: at 64 threads, the 128 row-block tasks split evenly two per thread, but at 256 threads half the threads sit idle since there aren't enough tasks to go around—and this affects both kernels equally, so that alone doesn't explain the gap.\n\nLooking closer, I think it's a B-reuse problem: the new kernel's packed B tile only gets reused across 4 row-quads per task, versus 16 rows of reuse in the simple kernel, so the new version streams roughly 4x more B traffic through memory. Bumping BI to 32 or 64 would improve reuse but shrinks the task count, hurting parallelism beyond that thread count—so I'm considering 2D tiling over both row and column blocks to balance reuse against task granularity, and I want to test a few BI values at 64 threads to see which wins.\n\n","time":{"start":1793101921716,"end":1793101928001},"metadata":{"anthropic":{"signature":""}}}}

{"type":"reasoning","timestamp":1793101994569,"sessionID":"ses_e82d0d703ffeCXd4cjTWZV8YjR","part":{"id":"prt_17d34fbc10010gvdAnB4QWYJk9","messageID":"msg_17d34f643001bbnqsTR3sSVr7S","sessionID":"ses_e82d0d703ffeCXd4cjTWZV8YjR","type":"reasoning","text":"I'm still puzzled why threads remain slower; noting that the simple kernel runs second in each rep so it may benefit from warmup, and the output only captures the last rep. Looking at 64-thread scaling, new achieves ~4 GFLOPS/thread versus simple's 372 total, which points me toward examining how the microkernel is called per i-quad, j-panel, k-tile combination.\n\nTracing the memory access pattern: A rows get reused from L1/L2 across j-panels, B panels of ~8KB per k-tile stay resident across quads, and the simple kernel reuses a larger B tile across 16 rows instead. C writes touch only a few cache lines per tile, so that seems negligible, and row blocks are large enough that false sharing between threads isn't likely the culprit. I'm now wondering if the 256 \"CPUs\" are actually hyperthreads sharing FMA ports, which would hurt the compute-bound new kernel more than the memory-bound simple one under multithreading, though that doesn't explain why new wins at 1 thread but loses at 64.\n\nI suspect L3 contention is a bigger factor — the new kernel's packed B buffer plus A and B themselves likely exceed L3 capacity, creating more traffic than the simple kernel's direct B reads. Given how much time I've spent and the noisy shared-machine load, I'll run one more bounded experiment: repeat the BI=16 vs BI=32 thread-scaling test three times at 64 threads to separate real signal from noise before deciding.\n\n","time":{"start":1793101986753,"end":1793101994526},"metadata":{"anthropic":{"signature":""}}}}
